# EU AI Act Logging Requirements: Articles 12, 19 and 26 Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/eu-ai-act-logging-requirements/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Article 12 of the EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to record events automatically over their lifetime; Articles 19 and 26 require providers and deployers to keep those logs for at least six months, and financial institutions to hold them within their financial services documentation. The Digital Omnibus moved the start date for Annex III systems to 2 December 2027 but left the logging text unchanged.

Under the EU AI Act, Article 12 requires high-risk AI systems to record events automatically over their lifetime, and Articles 19 and 26 require providers and deployers to keep those logs for at least six months. Financial institutions keep them within their financial services documentation. For Annex III systems such as credit scoring, the duties apply from 2 December 2027.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

The EU AI Act's logging rules are short, and most of the work they create is design work. The Act says what logs are for and how long to keep them; it leaves most of the content to the provider. This explainer reads the three articles closely and shows what they mean for a bank or insurer. Our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) sets these duties against FINRA, SEC, FCA and DORA expectations.

This page quotes the Commission's consolidated text and labelled secondary readings. It is not legal advice.

## Which EU AI Act articles cover logging?

Three articles. Article 12 sets the technical capability, Article 19 sets the provider's retention duty and Article 26 sets the deployer's.

| Article | Who it binds | What it requires | Retention | Financial institutions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12 Record-keeping | The high-risk system, and so its provider at the design stage | Automatic event logs over the system's lifetime, sufficient for traceability "appropriate to the intended purpose" | Not set here | No special rule |
| 19 Automatically generated logs | Providers | Keep logs generated by their systems "to the extent such logs are under their control" | At least six months, unless other law provides otherwise | Keep logs "as part of the documentation kept under the relevant financial services law" |
| 26(6) Obligations of deployers | Deployers | Keep logs generated by the system, where under their control | At least six months, unless other law provides otherwise | Keep logs within the documentation required by financial services law |
| 26(5) Obligations of deployers | Deployers | Monitor operation against the instructions for use; report risks and serious incidents | Not applicable | Monitoring duty treated as met by complying with financial services governance rules |
| 18 Documentation keeping | Providers | Keep technical, quality and conformity documentation | 10 years after placing on the market | Keep technical documentation within financial services documentation |

## What does Article 12 require?

It requires a capability, not a log format. Article 12(1) says high-risk systems "shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system."

Article 12(2) says the logging must ensure "a level of traceability of the functioning" that is "appropriate to the intended purpose of the system." It must record events relevant for:

- "identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk" under Article 79(1), "or in a substantial modification";
- "facilitating the post-market monitoring referred to in Article 72"; and
- "monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5)."

Article 72 adds context: providers must "actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data" on performance over the system's lifetime, including, where relevant, "interaction with other AI systems."

## What must the logs contain?

For most financial uses, the Act sets no field list. Article 12(3) lists minimum contents only for remote biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1(a): the period of each use, the reference database checked, the input data that matched, and the people who verified the results.

A creditworthiness system under Annex III point 5(b) gets the purposes in Article 12(2) and nothing more specific. The provider has to decide which events show a risk situation, support post-market monitoring and let the deployer monitor operation. In our reading, that usually means each run's inputs, model version, output, the human who acted on it and any override.

Standards may fill the gap later. The only harmonised standard published so far, EN 18286 on 14 October 2026, covers quality management, according to Orrick's 27 October reading; record-keeping and logging is one of ten areas in the Commission's standardisation request. VDE described ISO/IEC 24970, AI system logging, as a draft standard under development in December 2025. Our [AI audit trail checklist](https://lowob.com/research/ai-audit-trail-checklist/) gives a field list that covers the Article 12 purposes.

## How long must AI Act logs be kept?

At least six months, and often longer. Articles 19(1) and 26(6) both set a period "appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in the applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data."

That clause cuts both ways. Sector rules may require longer retention, and data protection law may require deletion or minimisation. A log that stores full customer inputs needs a retention rule and a deletion rule, agreed with the data protection officer.

## What changes for banks and insurers?

Their logs move into the documentation they already keep. Article 19(2) says providers that are financial institutions "shall maintain the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as part of the documentation kept under the relevant financial services law." Article 26(6) says the same for deployers.

Two further provisions matter. Under Article 26(5), a financial institution deployer's monitoring duty is treated as fulfilled by complying with its governance arrangements under financial services law. Under Article 72(4), providers that are financial institutions may integrate post-market monitoring for Annex III point 5 systems into their existing arrangements. In practice the AI Act floor of six months sits beneath longer sector periods.

The high-risk uses most likely in finance are Annex III point 5(b), systems "to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score", excluding fraud detection, and point 5(c), risk assessment and pricing for natural persons "in the case of life and health insurance."

## When do the logging duties apply?

From 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, according to White & Case.

The Omnibus moved dates, not logging text. The Commission's AI Act Service Desk marks Omnibus changes as NEW or AMENDED; none appears on Articles 12, 19 or 26 in the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. By contrast, Article 11 on technical documentation carries an amendment marker, and White & Case notes that the Omnibus extended SME relief such as simplified technical documentation. Our [EU AI Act for commercial teams](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/) sets out the full timetable.

## lowob takeaways

- **Article 12 sets purposes, not fields.** Outside remote biometric identification, the provider designs what the log records.
- **Six months is a floor.** Sector rules usually require longer; data protection law may require less personal data.
- **Financial firms fold logs into existing records.** Articles 19(2) and 26(6) route logs into financial services documentation.
- **The dates moved; the text did not.** Annex III duties apply from 2 December 2027 with the logging articles unchanged.

## Common questions

### What does Article 12 of the EU AI Act require?

Article 12 requires high-risk AI systems to technically allow automatic recording of events, or logs, over their lifetime. The logs must give traceability appropriate to the system's purpose and record events relevant to identifying risk situations or substantial modifications, supporting post-market monitoring under Article 72, and letting deployers monitor operation under Article 26(5). Specific minimum fields apply only to remote biometric identification.

### How long must AI logs be kept under the EU AI Act?

Providers under Article 19 and deployers under Article 26(6) must keep logs under their control for a period appropriate to the system's intended purpose, of at least six months, unless other EU or national law provides otherwise, in particular data protection law. Financial institutions keep the logs as part of the documentation required by EU financial services law.

### When do EU AI Act logging requirements apply to credit scoring?

From 2 December 2027. The Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and moved Annex III high-risk obligations, which include creditworthiness evaluation and credit scoring of natural persons, to that date. The Commission's consolidated text shows no amendments to the logging duties in Articles 12, 19 and 26.

### Do deployers have to keep AI Act logs?

Yes, for high-risk systems. Article 26(6) requires deployers to keep logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent the logs are under their control, for at least six months unless other law provides otherwise. Deployers must also monitor operation against the provider's instructions and inform the provider and authorities of risks and serious incidents.
